response.text:
I'll systematically compare source passages against the draft, hunting for signature-weight material that is absent, paraphrased away, or flattened.

**Key findings:**

1. **"What could they do if they were there? The surgeon has his round of thirty miles, and sleeps at Cranford; but every man cannot be a surgeon."** — The rhetorical question + the surgeon aside is a voice-establishing digression that the draft excises entirely, collapsing straight to the list. The ironic framing of "What could they do?" is the narrator's consciousness at work.

2. **The esprit de corps / Mrs Forrester paragraph** — The draft retains the Mrs Forrester scene but drops the framing sentence: "The Cranfordians had that kindly *esprit de corps* which made them overlook all deficiencies in success when some among them tried to conceal their poverty." The "second table, with housekeeper and steward, instead of the one little charity-school maiden" clause survives only partially — the draft strips "our hostess had a regular servants' hall, second table, with housekeeper and steward" and the full ironic buildup, cutting directly to the triple-nested "she knew that we knew."

3. **"I was surprised to hear his opinions quoted as authority at a visit which I paid to Cranford about a year after he had settled in the town... now he was even admitted in the tabooed hours before twelve. True, it was to discover the cause of a smoking chimney..."** — This entire passage showing the stages of Captain Brown's social rehabilitation is cut. It's interpretively critical: it demonstrates how Cranford society works (grudging, incremental acceptance; the smoking chimney as social pretext), and the narrator's ironic observation is signature voice.

4. **"He had been blind to all the small slights... He had been friendly, though the Cranford ladies had been cool; he had answered small sarcastic compliments in good faith; and with his manly frankness had overpowered all the shrinking which met him as a man who was not ashamed to be poor."** — This is entirely absent. It is interpretively crucial characterisation of Captain Brown and a sustained ironic passage with distinctive rhythm.

5. **The church scene** — The entire church scene (Captain Brown holding his double eye-glass, singing out loud and joyfully, the clerk with his piping feeble voice quivering higher and higher) is absent. This is a strongly individuated, comic scene establishing character.

6. **The Miss Jessie shopkeeper's uncle scene** — "Miss Jenkyns tried to drown this confession by a terrible cough—for the Honourable Mrs Jamieson was sitting at a card-table nearest Miss Jessie, and what would she say or think if she found out she was in the same room with a shop-keeper's niece!" — This is the ironic class comedy at full pitch. The draft omits it entirely, jumping from Miss Jessie's singing straight to the wine-and-biscuits. A major voice-establishing comic passage is erased.

7. **"Just allow me to read you a scene out of this month's number"** — The negotiation / "As you please, said she, settling herself with an air of resignation" is absent from the draft. This stage-direction irony is signature.

8. **The Miss Brown characterization** — "Her face, and there will be, I think, till she dies, though she should live to a hundred" (of Miss Jessie) is cut, as is the extended physical description of Miss Jessie's face (nose unformed and snub, lips red and dewy, rows of curls). "I do not know whether she was pretty or not; but I liked her face, and so did everybody, and I do not think she could help her dimples." This passage is frequently quoted and interpretively important.
